summary: The Moon has no global magnetic field and almost no atmosphere, so the solar wind strikes the surface directly and charges the dust. Charged dust can levitate and spark on suits and rovers; sunlight and UV help discharge it, but permanently shadowed regions have no easy discharge path.
title: Static charging and dust

summary: New craters form about 33% faster than scientists previously expected, so the surface is reworked more often than old maps assumed. Ejecta from an impact can travel at about 500 m/s, far beyond the crater rim.
title: Fresh impacts

summary: In direct sunlight the surface reaches about +127 °C, and in the dark it falls to about −173 °C. A lander must survive both, and the long dark stretch is when its batteries are tested most.
title: Thermal extremes

summary: With almost no atmosphere and no global magnetic field, radiation from the Sun and deep space reaches the surface directly. There is no air to slow it down and no magnetosphere to deflect it.
title: Thin air, weak shield
